entities.name: Juan Boscán Almogáver
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Juan Boscán Almogáver (died 1542), a Catalan poet writing primarily in Castilian, fundamentally reshaped Spanish poetry by introducing Italianate verse forms, most notably the hendecasyllable (undecasyllable), into the Castilian poetic tradition. Collaborating closely with his friend Garcilaso de la Vega, Boscán spearheaded a literary revolution that broke from medieval octosyllabic conventions, laying the groundwork for the Spanish Golden Age of literature. His innovation, inspired by the Renaissance humanism permeating Italy, profoundly influenced subsequent generations of Iberian poets and established a new metric and stylistic paradigm for the burgeoning Spanish language.

Born into a noble family in Barcelona, Boscán initially composed poetry in the traditional Castilian style. His pivotal encounter occurred around 1526 with Andrea Navagero, the Venetian ambassador to the court of Emperor Charles V, who encouraged Boscán to experiment with Italian forms. This intellectual catalyst led Boscán to adapt the hendecasyllable, the sonnet, the octave, and the terza rima, translating them into Castilian while maintaining their inherent musicality and structure. His most significant work, *Las obras de Boscán y algunas de Garcilaso de la Vega*, published posthumously in 1543 by his widow, doña Ana Girón de Rebolledo, became the foundational text for the new poetic movement. He also translated Baldassare Castiglione's influential *Il Cortegiano* (The Courtier) into Spanish in 1534, a work that defined the ideals of Renaissance courtly behavior and literary style.

entities.name: Juan Boscán Almogáver
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Juan Boscán Almogáver (1490, Barcelona – September 21, 1542), a pivotal figure in Spanish Renaissance literature, fundamentally reshaped Castilian poetry by introducing Italianate verse forms, particularly the hendecasyllable and the sonnet. His innovations, alongside his close friend Garcilaso de la Vega, marked a decisive break from medieval poetic traditions, ushering in a new era of lyrical expression that aligned Spain with the broader European Renaissance. He was not merely an adaptor but a champion who navigated initial resistance to these foreign forms, ultimately integrating them into the Spanish literary canon and fostering a new aesthetic sensibility.

Boscán's transformative encounter with Italian poetry occurred around 1526, influenced by Andrea Navagero, the Venetian ambassador to Spain, who encouraged him to experiment with hendecasyllabic verse. Prior to this, Spanish poetry was largely dominated by octosyllabic and dodecasyllabic lines, often in traditional ballad (romance) or *cancionero* forms. Boscán's work, notably *Las obras de Boscán y algunas de Garcilaso de la Vega, repartidas en quatro libros* (published posthumously in 1543), showcased his mastery of the sonnet, the octave, the tercet, and the *canción* (ode) in the Italian style. His acclaimed translation of Baldassare Castiglione's *Il Cortegiano* (1534) into Spanish prose further demonstrated his commitment to Renaissance humanism and provided a model for elegant Castilian prose, influencing courtly ideals and language for generations.
